The End of "Untouchables"

The appointment of Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla as the new Ombudsman comes at a time when the country’s trust in its institutions, and in the Marcos administration’s reform agenda, is being tested. His entry into this constitutional post signals not just continuity in the fight against corruption, but a renewed promise that justice will not bow to power.

Remulla’s track record speaks volumes. Under his watch at the Department of Justice, Rep. Arnie Teves was brought home to face charges, Apollo Quiboloy was forced out of hiding, and Atong Ang received his subpoena -- proof that for him, no one is untouchable. “No matter how high or mighty, if you err, you must be held accountable,” has been the quiet principle guiding his every move.

His experience in both the legislative and executive branches gives him a rare, panoramic view of governance. He knows where corruption festers and how it can be dismantled. As DOJ chief, he strengthened the National Prosecution Service, pushed for digital case management, and raised conviction rates. He also championed reforms in the Bureau of Corrections, seeking humane conditions and reduced congestion in jails.

Remulla’s reformist approach extended to human rights and transparency. He admitted the justice system’s shortcomings during the previous drug war and signaled openness to cooperate with the International Criminal Court under defined national terms, showing that accountability and sovereignty can coexist. His leadership earned him an 87.3% public satisfaction rating and recognition as Asia’s Outstanding Leader in Public Service.

Now, as Ombudsman, Remulla brings not only institutional experience but a clear moral compass. His appointment was vetted by the Judicial and Bar Council, affirming his integrity, competence, and fitness for office.

For the Marcos administration, his appointment could be a turning point. With Remulla as Ombudsman, the government gains a credible and independent partner in ensuring that public trust and transparency anchor its legacy. His presence reinforces the administration’s message that good governance and accountability are not mere slogans, but standards that can be enforced.

At the Ombudsman’s Office, Remulla’s challenge is both monumental and familiar: to ensure that the law shields the people, not the powerful. But if his past is any guide, he will confront corruption head-on, reform with precision, and pursue accountability without fear or favor.

In the end, Boying Remulla’s legacy may well define the success of this administration’s promise to clean up government, proof that justice, indeed, still works in the Philippines.

Godspeed Ombudsman Boying Remulla! 😎
